In 2016, Sepsis-3 was introduced to provide a more precise and standardized approach to the diagnosis and management of sepsis, emphasizing the presence of life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by an unregulated host response to infection (4). Specifically, it uses the Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) score to identify organ dysfunction, with an increase of 2 or more points in the qSOFA score indicating a potential sepsis diagnosis. An ideal biomarker for sepsis should be highly sensitive and specific, easily measurable, and capable of provid- ing real-time information about the patient’s condition (5,6). Over recent years, multiple biomarkers have been pro- posed and investigated for their potential roles in sepsis management. These include traditional biomarkers such as C-reactive protein (CRP) and procalcitonin (PCT), along with newer candidates like presepsin, soluble triggering receptor expressed on myeloid cells-1 (sTREM-1), and various cytokines and chemokines. Given the complex in- teractions between the host immune system and invading pathogens in sepsis, it is unlikely that a single biomarker can capture the full spectrum of the disease. Consequent- ly, recent studies have focused on integrated diagnostic approaches combining multi-biomarker panels with clinical evaluation and laboratory measurements (6). This review provides a comprehensive examination of the current status of sepsis biomarkers, highlighting their biological significance, diagnostic performance, and clini- cal utility. It discusses the strengths and limitations of individual biomarkers and explores emerging trends in bio- marker discovery and validation. Additionally, the potential of combining biomarkers with advanced technologies such as genomics, proteomics, and metabolomics to improve diagnostic and prognostic accuracy in sepsis will be ex- plored. RESULTS 1. Established biomarkers of sepsis 1) Procalcitonin (1) Mechanisms of action In sepsis, the rapid elevation of PCT levels is attributed to the host’s systemic inflammatory response to bacterial infection. Under normal conditions, PCT is produced in the thyroid and converted to calcitonin, playing no significant role in inflammatory processes. However, during bacterial infections, inflammatory cytokines like tumor necrosis fac- tor-α (TNF-α) and interleukin-6 (IL-6), along with bacte- rial endotoxins such as lipopolysaccharides, stimulate PCT production in multiple organs, bypassing thyroid regulation (7). This induction, primarily mediated by gene activation of the calcitonin gene-related peptide, results in a sharp in- crease in PCT that reflects the infection severity and over- all inflammatory burden. Notably, PCT levels remain low during viral infections, highlighting its specificity for bacte- rial pathogens and distinguishing it from other markers of systemic inflammation, such as CRP (8). (2) Clinical applications The clinical relevance of PCT spans multiple aspects of sepsis management, including diagnosis, therapeutic monitoring, and prognostic evaluation. Elevated PCT levels serve as a specific indicator of bacterial infections, making it an effective marker for early sepsis detection, especially in distinguishing bacterial infections from viral or other non-infectious causes of inflammation. Clinically, PCT’s half-life (about 24 hours) aligns well with infection dynam- ics, allowing for serial monitoring to assess therapeutic response and infection resolution. In the initial stages of sepsis, PCT levels rise rapidly, enabling early intervention. PCT’s specificity for bacterial infections offers a diagnos- tic advantage over other inflammatory markers, reducing the likelihood of misdiagnosis and unnecessary treatment in cases where bacterial involvement is not present (9). Beyond its diagnostic utility, PCT play a significant role in antibiotic stewardship. By monitoring PCT levels, clini- Kyeong Seob Shin 226 BSL 2025;31(3):225-235 BSL

--- Page 3 --- cians can make informed decisions about initiating or dis- continuing antibiotics. For example, a declining PCT level indicates a positive response to treatment, suggesting the possibility of safely reducing or stopping antibiotic therapy. This practice helps minimize the duration of antibiotic exposure, reducing the risk of developing resistance and decreasing healthcare costs (10). Additionally, PCT provide valuable prognostic information, as its levels have been shown to correlate with disease severity and mortality risk in sepsis patients. Persistently high or increasing PCT levels despite treatment are associated with poorer out- comes and greater risk of complications. Thus, PCT can help stratify patients based on risk and inform decisions about escalation of care (11). (3) Diagnostic performance as a biomarker Numerous studies affirm PCT’s high diagnostic perfor- mance, with reported sensitivity ranging from 65%–75% and specificity from 70%–80% for bacterial sepsis (9). Al- though PCT alone provides strong diagnostic support, it is often used in conjunction with CRP and other markers to enhance diagnostic accuracy and improve patient out- comes. The combination of PCT with clinical assessments and other biomarkers yields a robust framework for early diagnosis, timely treatment, and dynamic monitoring of sepsis progression (9). Nevertheless, PCT may also rise in certain non-infectious conditions such as major trauma, surgery, or prolonged cardiogenic shock, which limits its absolute specificity for bacterial infection. 2) C-reactive protein CRP is an acute-phase protein elevated in response to systemic inflammation, especially during sepsis, due to cytokine-driven hepatic synthesis. It aids in immune response by binding to pathogen surfaces, activating the complement system, and promoting opsonization. Clini- cally, CRP assists in diagnosing and monitoring sepsis progression, although it lacks specificity for bacterial in- fection. Its levels can guide antibiotic therapy and provide prognostic insights, but it is most effective when used alongside other biomarkers, such as PCT, to enhance di- agnostic accuracy in sepsis management. (1) Mechanisms of action CRP is an acute-phase protein predominantly syn- thesized by the liver in response to pro-inflammatory cytokines, particularly IL-6, TNF-α, and IL-1β (12). During sepsis, the inflammatory response triggers hepatocytes to produce and release CRP into the bloodstream, leading to elevated CRP levels within hours of infection onset. This rapid elevation serves as a marker of systemic inflamma- tion. CRP plays a role in the immune response by bind- ing to phosphocholine on pathogen surfaces, promoting opsonization, and activating the complement system. Elevated CRP levels reflect systemic inflammation but are not specific to bacterial infection alone, as CRP can rise in other inflammatory conditions. (2) Clinical applications In sepsis management, CRP is commonly used for diag- nosis, guiding antibiotic therapy, and assessing prognosis. As a diagnostic tool, CRP levels above 10 mg/L indicate a heightened inflammatory response, with levels often ex- ceeding 100 mg/L in severe infections like sepsis (13). CRP can aid in early identification but lacks specificity for bac- terial versus viral infections. In guiding antibiotic therapy, CRP can help clinicians monitor response to treatment; a reduction in CRP over 48–72 hours often suggests a favorable response, allowing for potential adjustments in therapy duration. Prognostically, persistently high or rising CRP levels are associated with poor outcomes and may indicate worsening sepsis or inadequate infection control (14). (3) Diagnostic performance While CRP is widely used due to its sensitivity to in- flammation, its specificity in sepsis is limited. CRP’s sen- sitivity generally exceeds 90% for detecting inflammatory conditions, including sepsis, but specificity is often lower (50%–70%) since it can elevate in non-bacterial infec- Biomarker for Sepsis 227 https://doi.org/10.15616/BSL.2025.31.3.225 BSL

--- Page 4 --- tions and other non-infectious inflammatory states (e.g., trauma, surgery) (13). Compared to biomarkers like PCT, CRP lacks the ability to specifically distinguish bacterial in- fection in sepsis, though it provides valuable insight when used alongside clinical assessment and other biomarkers (15). Thus, CRP alone is insufficient for sepsis diagnosis, but it complements PCT and other biomarker to enhance diagnostic confidence and therapeutic monitoring. 3) Biomarker for sepsis: cytokines Cytokines play a central role in the dysregulated hot immune response during sepsis. Their rapid release and dynamic balance between pro- and anti-inflammatory mediators not only drive the pathophysiology of sepsis but also provide valuable insights for early diagnosis and prog- nosis. As such, several cytokines have been investigated as potential biomarkers in sepsis management (5). (1) Interleukin-6 ① Mechanism of action IL-6 is a multifunctional cytokine that plays a pivotal role in the immune response during sepsis. It is produced by monocytes, macrophages, and endothelial cells in re- sponse to infection and tissue damage. IL-6 stimulates the liver to produce acute-phase proteins, including CRP, thus linking inflammation to systemic physiological re- sponses. It also aids in lymphocyte differentiation and reg- ulates the balance between pro-inflammatory and anti- inflammatory responses (16). ② Clinical application IL-6 is widely used as a biomarker for early detection and monitoring of sepsis due to its rapid increase in re- sponse to infection. Elevated IL-6 levels are associated with increased severity of sepsis and poorer outcomes. Monitoring IL-6 levels over time can help clinicians assess the progression or resolution of sepsis, guiding treatment decisions and helping to identify high-risk patients (17). ③ Diagnostic performance IL-6 shows high sensitivity in detecting sepsis, often rising earlier than CRP or PCT, making it suitable for early diagnosis. However, because IL-6 can be elevated in a variety of inflammatory conditions, its specificity for sepsis is limited (18). To improve diagnostic accuracy, IL-6 is fre- quently used alongside other biomarkers, such as PCT or CRP, to enhance specificity in differentiating sepsis from other inflammatory conditions. However, since IL-6 can be elevated in autoimmune disease, trauma, or other sys- temic inflammatory states, its specificity is limited and it is best together with other markers such as PCT. (2) Tumor necrosis factor-α ① Mechanism of action TNF-α is a pro-inflammatory cytokine primarily pro- duced by activated macrophages and monocytes. It ini- tiates a cascade of inflammatory responses in sepsis, leading to increased vascular permeability, hypotension, and the recruitment of additional immune cells to the site of infection (19). TNF-α is one of the earliest cytokines re- leased in response to infection, amplifying the inflamma- tory response and potentially leading to tissue injury and organ dysfunction in severe sepsis cases. ② Clinical application TNF-α’s role in initiating the inflammatory cascade makes it a valuable marker for understanding the patho- physiology of sepsis. While TNF-α is not commonly used as a standalone diagnostic biomarker due to its short half- life and rapid clearance from circulation, it is crucial in re- search settings to elucidate early inflammatory changes. In clinical practice, TNF-α levels are often assessed along- side other cytokines to monitor the intensity of the inflam- matory response in patients with severe sepsis or septic shock (20). ③ Diagnostic performance TNF-α levels rise very early in the course of sepsis, pro- viding initial insight into the inflammatory status of the pa- tient. However, its short half-life limits its routine use as a diagnostic marker, as levels can quickly return to baseline even in active sepsis. Additionally, TNF-α lacks specificity, Kyeong Seob Shin 228 BSL 2025;31(3):225-235 BSL

--- Page 5 --- as it may be elevated in other inflammatory or infectious diseases. Thus, while valuable in research, TNF-α is rarely used as a primary diagnostic biomarker in clinical settings (21). Due to its short half-life and lack of specificity, TNF-α is rarely adopted in routine clinical practice and remains primarily of research interest. (3) Interleukin-8 ① Mechanism of action IL-8 is a chemokine that plays a crucial role in neutrophil activation and recruitment to the site of infection. Dur- ing sepsis, IL-8 levels surge, guiding neutrophils to the infection site, where they contribute to pathogen clear- ance (22). This recruitment of immune cells is essential for containing and eliminating infection, but an excessive IL-8 response can lead to an overwhelming inflammatory re- sponse, contributing to tissue damage. ② Clinical application IL-8 is valuable in assessing the immune response’s severity and helps predict outcomes in sepsis patients. Elevated IL-8 levels are often correlated with the severity of sepsis, and high levels are linked with poorer outcomes, such as organ dysfunction or mortality. Measuring IL-8 can be helpful in triaging sepsis patients and monitoring response to treatment, particularly in critically ill patients (23). ③ Diagnostic performance IL-8 shows promise as a biomarker due to its sensitiv- ity to bacterial infections and its rapid response in early sepsis stages. However, like TNF-α, IL-8 can be elevated in other inflammatory conditions, which limits its specific- ity (24). Therefore, IL-8 is often measured alongside other markers, such as PCT or CRP, to improve diagnostic accu- racy and to differentiate between sepsis and other inflam- matory states. (4) Interleukin-10 ① Mechanism of action IL-10 is an anti-inflammatory cytokine produced by reg- ulatory T-cells, macrophages, and monocytes in response to inflammation. In sepsis, IL-10 acts as a counter- regulatory mechanism to mitigate the pro-inflammatory response, helping to prevent excessive tissue damage (25). It downregulates the production of pro-inflammatory cy- tokines, such as TNF-α and IL-1, contributing to immune homeostasis. However, persistently elevated IL-10 levels can indicate immune suppression, which may increase susceptibility to secondary infections and worsen sepsis outcomes. ② Clinical application IL-10 is often used as a prognostic marker rather than a diagnostic one, as high levels are associated with an increased risk of mortality and immune dysregulation in sepsis patients (26). Monitoring IL-10 can provide insights into the balance between pro- and anti-inflammatory re- sponses, helping clinicians to assess the immune status of patients. Elevated IL-10 may also signal the need for closer monitoring and more aggressive therapeutic inter- ventions. ③ Diagnostic performance IL-10’s role as an anti-inflammatory cytokine makes it less useful for diagnosing sepsis compared to pro-inflam- matory markers. However, IL-10 is a valuable prognostic marker; elevated levels often correlate with poor prognosis and can indicate an overcompensated immune response, particularly in severe cases of sepsis (27). As a biomarker, IL-10 is most informative when used in conjunction with pro-inflammatory markers like IL-6, providing a more comprehensive picture of the immune response in sep- sis. IL-10 is there better regarded as a prognostic marker of immune dysregulation rather than a diagnostic tool for sepsis. Recent studies have therefore focused on emerging biomarkers that can provide earlier detection, better prognostic information, and more precise risk stratification in sepsis. These promising candi- dates include sTREM-1, proadrenomedullin (ProADM), and heparin-binding protein (HBP), among others (5,6). 1) Soluble triggering receptor expressed on myeloid cells-1 (1) Mechanism of action sTREM-1 is expressed on the surface of neutrophils and monocytes, becoming activated in response to infection. When an infection is present, sTREM-1 is released into the bloodstream, amplifying the inflammatory response. It plays a key role in modulating immune responses in sepsis by promoting cell-mediated immune reactions and induc- ing cytokine release (28). (2) Clinical utility sTREM-1 is valuable for differentiating the presence of infection and assessing the severity of the inflammatory response. It aids in early diagnosis of sepsis by helping to distinguish infectious sepsis from non-infectious inflam- matory conditions. (3) Diagnostic performance sTREM-1 demonstrates high sensitivity and specific- ity, making it a promising biomarker for sepsis diagnosis. Supporting evidence indicates that sTREM-1 is specifically upregulated in bacterial infection, while sterile inflam- mation such as trauma or postoperative stress produces minimal activation, which underlies its ability to distinguish infectious from non-infectious conditions. However, it is recommended to use it alongside other biomarkers (such as PCT and CRP) to improve diagnostic accuracy. 2) Proadrenomedullin (1) Mechanism of action ProADM is the precursor of adrenomedullin, a hor- mone essential for vascular regulation and inflammatory response. During sepsis, ProADM levels rise due to in- creased vascular permeability and excessive inflammatory activation (29). (2) Clinical utility ProADM reflects endothelial function and overall hemo- dynamic status, making it useful for prognosis and severity assessment in sepsis patients. Elevated ProADM levels in acute infections are associated with worse clinical out- comes. (3) Diagnostic performance ProADM is better suited for prognosis rather than diag- nosis in sepsis. Although not specific for infection, ProADM provides incremental value by reflecting endo- thelial dysfunction and circulatory stress, which are central features of severe sepsis and septic shock. 3) Heparin-binding protein (1) Mechanism of action HBP is a protein released by activated neutrophils, sig- nificantly increasing vascular permeability. During inflam- mation, it facilitates protein translocation across vascular walls, contributing to endothelial damage and the devel- opment of shock (30). (2) Clinical utility HBP is valuable for early prediction of septic shock, particularly for detecting severe circulatory disturbances related to sepsis. HBP levels increase early in infection, providing crucial information for rapid sepsis diagnosis and treatment. (3) Diagnostic performance HBP is highly predictive of septic shock, showing high diagnostic performance in this context. Elevated HBP lev- els in patients with suspected infection signal a higher risk for septic shock, proving its usefulness in early risk as- sessment. Its ability to predict progression to septic shock makes HBP particularly useful in the emergency setting for early triage of high-risk patients. 4) Neutrophil gelatinase-associated lipocalin (1) Mechanism of action Neutrophil gelatinase-associated lipocalin (NGAL) is a protein secreted by neutrophils and renal tubular epithelial cells. It rapidly increases during acute kidney injury (AKI) and reflects neutrophil activation in infection and inflam- mation (31). (2) Clinical utility NGAL is most valuable for early detection of AKI in sep- sis, often rising 24–48 hours before creatinine. It aids in assessing sepsis severity and complications, particularly renal dysfunction, and supports risk stratification in pa- tients admitted to the intensive care unit (32). (3) Diagnostic performance For AKI detection, NGAL demonstrates an area under the curve (AUC) of approximately 0.75–0.85. While less specific for diagnosing sepsis itself, NGAL provides high clinical value for predicting and monitoring sepsis-associ- ated complications (33). 5) Presepsin (sCD14-ST) (1) Mechanism of action Presepsin is a soluble fragment of CD14, released dur- ing activation of monocytes and macrophages in response to bacterial infection. It reflects early immune activation, particularly through the LPS-CD14-TLR4 signaling path- way (34). (2) Clinical utility Presepsin is valuable for early diagnosis of bacterial sepsis, often rising more rapidly than PCT. It also supports severity classification (distinguishing sepsis from septic shock) and has shown usefulness in neonatal and pediat- ric sepsis (35). (3) Diagnostic performance Meta-analyses have reported an AUC of approximately 0.80–0.85, with sensitivity and specificity comparable to or exceeding those of PCT in some studies. Presepsin is particularly strong in early detection and prognostic as- sessment (36). Nevertheless, larger multicenter studies are still required to validate its cutoff values and standardize its clinical use. In 2016, Sepsis-3 was introduced to provide a more precise and standardized approach to the diagnosis and management of sepsis, emphasizing the presence of life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by an unregulated host response to infection (4). Specifically, it uses the Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) score to identify organ dysfunction, with an increase of 2 or more points in the qSOFA score indicating a potential sepsis diagnosis. An ideal biomarker for sepsis should be highly sensitive and specific, easily measurable, and capable of provid- ing real-time information about the patient’s condition (5,6). Over recent years, multiple biomarkers have been pro- posed and investigated for their potential roles in sepsis management. These include traditional biomarkers such as C-reactive protein (CRP) and procalcitonin (PCT), along with newer candidates like presepsin, soluble triggering receptor expressed on myeloid cells-1 (sTREM-1), and various cytokines and chemokines. Given the complex in- teractions between the host immune system and invading pathogens in sepsis, it is unlikely that a single biomarker can capture the full spectrum of the disease. Consequent- ly, recent studies have focused on integrated diagnostic approaches combining multi-biomarker panels with clinical evaluation and laboratory measurements (6). This review provides a comprehensive examination of the current status of sepsis biomarkers, highlighting their biological significance, diagnostic performance, and clini- cal utility. It discusses the strengths and limitations of individual biomarkers and explores emerging trends in bio- marker discovery and validation. Additionally, the potential of combining biomarkers with advanced technologies such as genomics, proteomics, and metabolomics to improve diagnostic and prognostic accuracy in sepsis will be ex- plored. RESULTS 1. Established biomarkers of sepsis 1) Procalcitonin (1) Mechanisms of action In sepsis, the rapid elevation of PCT levels is attributed to the host’s systemic inflammatory response to bacterial infection. Under normal conditions, PCT is produced in the thyroid and converted to calcitonin, playing no significant role in inflammatory processes. However, during bacterial infections, inflammatory cytokines like tumor necrosis fac- tor-α (TNF-α) and interleukin-6 (IL-6), along with bacte- rial endotoxins such as lipopolysaccharides, stimulate PCT production in multiple organs, bypassing thyroid regulation (7). This induction, primarily mediated by gene activation of the calcitonin gene-related peptide, results in a sharp in- crease in PCT that reflects the infection severity and over- all inflammatory burden. Notably, PCT levels remain low during viral infections, highlighting its specificity for bacte- rial pathogens and distinguishing it from other markers of systemic inflammation, such as CRP (8). (2) Clinical applications The clinical relevance of PCT spans multiple aspects of sepsis management, including diagnosis, therapeutic monitoring, and prognostic evaluation. Elevated PCT levels serve as a specific indicator of bacterial infections, making it an effective marker for early sepsis detection, especially in distinguishing bacterial infections from viral or other non-infectious causes of inflammation. Clinically, PCT’s half-life (about 24 hours) aligns well with infection dynam- ics, allowing for serial monitoring to assess therapeutic response and infection resolution. In the initial stages of sepsis, PCT levels rise rapidly, enabling early intervention. PCT’s specificity for bacterial infections offers a diagnos- tic advantage over other inflammatory markers, reducing the likelihood of misdiagnosis and unnecessary treatment in cases where bacterial involvement is not present (9). Beyond its diagnostic utility, PCT play a significant role in antibiotic stewardship. By monitoring PCT levels, clini- Kyeong Seob Shin 226 BSL 2025;31(3):225-235 BSL

--- Page 3 --- cians can make informed decisions about initiating or dis- continuing antibiotics. For example, a declining PCT level indicates a positive response to treatment, suggesting the possibility of safely reducing or stopping antibiotic therapy. This practice helps minimize the duration of antibiotic exposure, reducing the risk of developing resistance and decreasing healthcare costs (10). Additionally, PCT provide valuable prognostic information, as its levels have been shown to correlate with disease severity and mortality risk in sepsis patients. Persistently high or increasing PCT levels despite treatment are associated with poorer out- comes and greater risk of complications. Thus, PCT can help stratify patients based on risk and inform decisions about escalation of care (11). (3) Diagnostic performance as a biomarker Numerous studies affirm PCT’s high diagnostic perfor- mance, with reported sensitivity ranging from 65%–75% and specificity from 70%–80% for bacterial sepsis (9). Al- though PCT alone provides strong diagnostic support, it is often used in conjunction with CRP and other markers to enhance diagnostic accuracy and improve patient out- comes. The combination of PCT with clinical assessments and other biomarkers yields a robust framework for early diagnosis, timely treatment, and dynamic monitoring of sepsis progression (9). Nevertheless, PCT may also rise in certain non-infectious conditions such as major trauma, surgery, or prolonged cardiogenic shock, which limits its absolute specificity for bacterial infection. 2) C-reactive protein CRP is an acute-phase protein elevated in response to systemic inflammation, especially during sepsis, due to cytokine-driven hepatic synthesis. It aids in immune response by binding to pathogen surfaces, activating the complement system, and promoting opsonization. Clini- cally, CRP assists in diagnosing and monitoring sepsis progression, although it lacks specificity for bacterial in- fection. Its levels can guide antibiotic therapy and provide prognostic insights, but it is most effective when used alongside other biomarkers, such as PCT, to enhance di- agnostic accuracy in sepsis management. (1) Mechanisms of action CRP is an acute-phase protein predominantly syn- thesized by the liver in response to pro-inflammatory cytokines, particularly IL-6, TNF-α, and IL-1β (12). During sepsis, the inflammatory response triggers hepatocytes to produce and release CRP into the bloodstream, leading to elevated CRP levels within hours of infection onset. This rapid elevation serves as a marker of systemic inflamma- tion. CRP plays a role in the immune response by bind- ing to phosphocholine on pathogen surfaces, promoting opsonization, and activating the complement system. Elevated CRP levels reflect systemic inflammation but are not specific to bacterial infection alone, as CRP can rise in other inflammatory conditions. (2) Clinical applications In sepsis management, CRP is commonly used for diag- nosis, guiding antibiotic therapy, and assessing prognosis. As a diagnostic tool, CRP levels above 10 mg/L indicate a heightened inflammatory response, with levels often ex- ceeding 100 mg/L in severe infections like sepsis (13). CRP can aid in early identification but lacks specificity for bac- terial versus viral infections. In guiding antibiotic therapy, CRP can help clinicians monitor response to treatment; a reduction in CRP over 48–72 hours often suggests a favorable response, allowing for potential adjustments in therapy duration. Prognostically, persistently high or rising CRP levels are associated with poor outcomes and may indicate worsening sepsis or inadequate infection control (14). (3) Diagnostic performance While CRP is widely used due to its sensitivity to in- flammation, its specificity in sepsis is limited. CRP’s sen- sitivity generally exceeds 90% for detecting inflammatory conditions, including sepsis, but specificity is often lower (50%–70%) since it can elevate in non-bacterial infec- Biomarker for Sepsis 227 https://doi.org/10.15616/BSL.2025.31.3.225 BSL

--- Page 4 --- tions and other non-infectious inflammatory states (e.g., trauma, surgery) (13). Compared to biomarkers like PCT, CRP lacks the ability to specifically distinguish bacterial in- fection in sepsis, though it provides valuable insight when used alongside clinical assessment and other biomarkers (15). Thus, CRP alone is insufficient for sepsis diagnosis, but it complements PCT and other biomarker to enhance diagnostic confidence and therapeutic monitoring. 3) Biomarker for sepsis: cytokines Cytokines play a central role in the dysregulated hot immune response during sepsis. Their rapid release and dynamic balance between pro- and anti-inflammatory mediators not only drive the pathophysiology of sepsis but also provide valuable insights for early diagnosis and prog- nosis. As such, several cytokines have been investigated as potential biomarkers in sepsis management (5). (1) Interleukin-6 ① Mechanism of action IL-6 is a multifunctional cytokine that plays a pivotal role in the immune response during sepsis. It is produced by monocytes, macrophages, and endothelial cells in re- sponse to infection and tissue damage. IL-6 stimulates the liver to produce acute-phase proteins, including CRP, thus linking inflammation to systemic physiological re- sponses. It also aids in lymphocyte differentiation and reg- ulates the balance between pro-inflammatory and anti- inflammatory responses (16). ② Clinical application IL-6 is widely used as a biomarker for early detection and monitoring of sepsis due to its rapid increase in re- sponse to infection. Elevated IL-6 levels are associated with increased severity of sepsis and poorer outcomes. Monitoring IL-6 levels over time can help clinicians assess the progression or resolution of sepsis, guiding treatment decisions and helping to identify high-risk patients (17). ③ Diagnostic performance IL-6 shows high sensitivity in detecting sepsis, often rising earlier than CRP or PCT, making it suitable for early diagnosis. However, because IL-6 can be elevated in a variety of inflammatory conditions, its specificity for sepsis is limited (18). To improve diagnostic accuracy, IL-6 is fre- quently used alongside other biomarkers, such as PCT or CRP, to enhance specificity in differentiating sepsis from other inflammatory conditions. However, since IL-6 can be elevated in autoimmune disease, trauma, or other sys- temic inflammatory states, its specificity is limited and it is best together with other markers such as PCT. (2) Tumor necrosis factor-α ① Mechanism of action TNF-α is a pro-inflammatory cytokine primarily pro- duced by activated macrophages and monocytes. It ini- tiates a cascade of inflammatory responses in sepsis, leading to increased vascular permeability, hypotension, and the recruitment of additional immune cells to the site of infection (19). TNF-α is one of the earliest cytokines re- leased in response to infection, amplifying the inflamma- tory response and potentially leading to tissue injury and organ dysfunction in severe sepsis cases. ② Clinical application TNF-α’s role in initiating the inflammatory cascade makes it a valuable marker for understanding the patho- physiology of sepsis. While TNF-α is not commonly used as a standalone diagnostic biomarker due to its short half- life and rapid clearance from circulation, it is crucial in re- search settings to elucidate early inflammatory changes. In clinical practice, TNF-α levels are often assessed along- side other cytokines to monitor the intensity of the inflam- matory response in patients with severe sepsis or septic shock (20). ③ Diagnostic performance TNF-α levels rise very early in the course of sepsis, pro- viding initial insight into the inflammatory status of the pa- tient. However, its short half-life limits its routine use as a diagnostic marker, as levels can quickly return to baseline even in active sepsis. Recent studies have therefore focused on emerging biomarkers that can provide earlier detection, better prognostic information, and more precise risk stratification in sepsis. These promising candi- dates include sTREM-1, proadrenomedullin (ProADM), and heparin-binding protein (HBP), among others (5,6). 1) Soluble triggering receptor expressed on myeloid cells-1 (1) Mechanism of action sTREM-1 is expressed on the surface of neutrophils and monocytes, becoming activated in response to infection. When an infection is present, sTREM-1 is released into the bloodstream, amplifying the inflammatory response. It plays a key role in modulating immune responses in sepsis by promoting cell-mediated immune reactions and induc- ing cytokine release (28). (2) Clinical utility sTREM-1 is valuable for differentiating the presence of infection and assessing the severity of the inflammatory response. It aids in early diagnosis of sepsis by helping to distinguish infectious sepsis from non-infectious inflam- matory conditions. (3) Diagnostic performance sTREM-1 demonstrates high sensitivity and specific- ity, making it a promising biomarker for sepsis diagnosis. Supporting evidence indicates that sTREM-1 is specifically upregulated in bacterial infection, while sterile inflam- mation such as trauma or postoperative stress produces minimal activation, which underlies its ability to distinguish infectious from non-infectious conditions. However, it is recommended to use it alongside other biomarkers (such as PCT and CRP) to improve diagnostic accuracy. 2) Proadrenomedullin (1) Mechanism of action ProADM is the precursor of adrenomedullin, a hor- mone essential for vascular regulation and inflammatory response. During sepsis, ProADM levels rise due to in- creased vascular permeability and excessive inflammatory activation (29). (2) Clinical utility ProADM reflects endothelial function and overall hemo- dynamic status, making it useful for prognosis and severity assessment in sepsis patients. Elevated ProADM levels in acute infections are associated with worse clinical out- comes. (3) Diagnostic performance ProADM is better suited for prognosis rather than diag- nosis in sepsis. --- Page 7 --- markers, it can play a supportive role in early diagnosis and severity assessment. Although not specific for infection, ProADM provides incremental value by reflecting endo- thelial dysfunction and circulatory stress, which are central features of severe sepsis and septic shock. 3) Heparin-binding protein (1) Mechanism of action HBP is a protein released by activated neutrophils, sig- nificantly increasing vascular permeability. During inflam- mation, it facilitates protein translocation across vascular walls, contributing to endothelial damage and the devel- opment of shock (30). (2) Clinical utility HBP is valuable for early prediction of septic shock, particularly for detecting severe circulatory disturbances related to sepsis. HBP levels increase early in infection, providing crucial information for rapid sepsis diagnosis and treatment. (3) Diagnostic performance HBP is highly predictive of septic shock, showing high diagnostic performance in this context. Elevated HBP lev- els in patients with suspected infection signal a higher risk for septic shock, proving its usefulness in early risk as- sessment. Its ability to predict progression to septic shock makes HBP particularly useful in the emergency setting for early triage of high-risk patients. 4) Neutrophil gelatinase-associated lipocalin (1) Mechanism of action Neutrophil gelatinase-associated lipocalin (NGAL) is a protein secreted by neutrophils and renal tubular epithelial cells. It rapidly increases during acute kidney injury (AKI) and reflects neutrophil activation in infection and inflam- mation (31). (2) Clinical utility NGAL is most valuable for early detection of AKI in sep- sis, often rising 24–48 hours before creatinine. It aids in assessing sepsis severity and complications, particularly renal dysfunction, and supports risk stratification in pa- tients admitted to the intensive care unit (32). (3) Diagnostic performance For AKI detection, NGAL demonstrates an area under the curve (AUC) of approximately 0.75–0.85. While less specific for diagnosing sepsis itself, NGAL provides high clinical value for predicting and monitoring sepsis-associ- ated complications (33). 5) Presepsin (sCD14-ST) (1) Mechanism of action Presepsin is a soluble fragment of CD14, released dur- ing activation of monocytes and macrophages in response to bacterial infection. It reflects early immune activation, particularly through the LPS-CD14-TLR4 signaling path- way (34). (2) Clinical utility Presepsin is valuable for early diagnosis of bacterial sepsis, often rising more rapidly than PCT. It also supports severity classification (distinguishing sepsis from septic shock) and has shown usefulness in neonatal and pediat- ric sepsis (35). (3) Diagnostic performance Meta-analyses have reported an AUC of approximately 0.80–0.85, with sensitivity and specificity comparable to or exceeding those of PCT in some studies. Presepsin is particularly strong in early detection and prognostic as- sessment (36). Nevertheless, larger multicenter studies are still required to validate its cutoff values and standardize its clinical use. CONCLUSION Sepsis remains a major global health burden, and de- spite decades of research, its timely diagnosis and precise management remain challenging. Established biomarkers such as PCT and CRP are widely used in clinical practice, but their limited specificity and sensitivity underscore the need for additional tools. Cytokines including IL-6, TNF-α, and IL-10 provide valuable insights into the host immune response and disease severity, while emerging candidates such as sTREM-1, ProADM, and HBP show promise for improving early recognition and risk stratification. Never- theless, no single biomarker is sufficient to capture the complex pathophysiology of sepsis, which involves dys- regulated inflammation, immune suppression, endothe- lial dysfunction, and multi-organ injury. Future research should therefore prioritize integrated approaches that combine multiple biomarkers with clinical scoring system, imaging modalities, and advanced molecular technologies. Multi-marker panels, when interpreted in the context of patient characteristics and comorbidities, may enhance diagnostic accuracy, optimize therapeutic decisions such as antibiotic stewardship, and facilitate individualized prognostic assessment. Moreover, advances in high- throughput genomics, proteomics, and metabolomics are expected to identify novel biomarkers and generate per- sonalized sepsis signatures, enabling earlier intervention and reducing mortality. In conclusion, while significant progress has been made in the identification and validation of sepsis biomarkers, successful translation into routine practice will require rigorous validation in diverse populations, standardization of cutoff values, and incorporation into clinical algorithms. A concerted effort among researchers, clinicians, and policymakers will be essential to move from discovery to bedside application, ensuring that biomarker-driven ap- proaches meaningfully improve sepsis diagnosis, manage- ment, and prognosis. ABSTRACT Introduction The management of fever without source in children ≤36 months old remains a diagnostic challenge as the underlying aetiologies can vary from self-­limiting viral infections to serious bacterial infections (SBIs). Biomarkers such as C reactive protein (CRP), procalcitonin (PCT) and interleukin-­6 (IL-­6) have varying thresholds in the prediction of SBIs due to differences in SBI definitions, SBI prevalence, patient characteristics and timing of presentation. This protocol describes a systematic review and meta-­analysis that aims to determine the thresholds at which CRP, PCT and IL-­6 can perform optimally in distinguishing the presence of SBIs in children ≤36 months old, as well as to determine their performances in early detection of bacterial infections within 48 hours of fever onset. Methods and analysis We will systematically search electronic databases including MEDLINE, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, Cochrane CENTRAL, EMBASE, CINAHL (Cumulative Index to Nursing and Allied Health Literature) and Science Citation Index from 1 July 2023 to 31 July 2023. We will include studies that report the diagnostic accuracy of CRP, PCT and IL-­6 in detecting SBIs in children aged ≤36 months presenting with fever without apparent source. Randomised controlled trials (RCTs) and non-­randomised studies including non-­RCTs and controlled before-­and-­after studies will be included. A meta-­analysis will be performed and diagnostic performances of these biomarkers will be reported. Ethics and dissemination The results of this study will provide guidance on clinical decision-­making in young children presenting with fever without source. Ethics approval will not be required for this study. The authors aim to publish the findings in a peer-­reviewed journal as well as present at international conferences. PROSPERO registration number CRD42023439093. INTRODUCTION Rationale Fever without source, defined as fever less than 7 days without a clear source of infection, is one of the most common complaints in paediatric patients, representing approxi- mately 20% of febrile children presenting to the emergency department.1 It remains a diag- nostic challenge as the underlying aetiologies can vary, from self-­limiting viral infections to serious bacterial infections (SBIs) with long-­ term sequelae and mortality.2 It is particularly challenging in children ≤36 months of age as they often present without focal symptoms and may even appear well.3 Despite extensive history and physical examination, clinicians are often unable to identify a specific source in this population.4 The well-­appearing child WHAT IS ALREADY KNOWN ON THIS TOPIC ⇒Management of fever without source in young chil- dren remains unclear. ⇒Biomarkers such as C reactive protein (CRP), pro- calcitonin (PCT) and interleukin-­6 (IL-­6) have been well reported to accurately predict serious bacterial infections (SBIs). ⇒However, optimal diagnostic thresholds and utility for early detection are debated. WHAT THIS STUDY ADDS ⇒This protocol describes a systematic review and meta-­analysis that aims to determine the thresholds at which biomarkers such as CRP, PCT and IL-­6 can accurately predict the presence of SBIs in children ≤36 months old, and to determine their diagnostic performances in early detection of bacterial infec- tions within 48 hours of fever onset. HOW THIS STUDY MIGHT AFFECT RESEARCH, PRACTICE OR POLICY ⇒The findings of this study will provide guidance on clinical decision-­making in young children present- ing with fever without source. The risk of missed diagnosis often leads to inappropriate prescribing of antibiotics, hospital admissions and unnecessary invasive testing.5 This clinical conundrum has led to an increasing volume of research into the role of biomarkers that aid clinicians in accurate and early diagnosis of SBIs. Among the biomarkers that have been evaluated, C reactive protein (CRP) and procalcitonin (PCT) have consistently been reported to be reliable predictors of SBIs in paediatric patients.6 7 Newer studies have also proposed the emerging role of cytokines, such as interleukin-­6 (IL-­6), in predicting sepsis in young chil- dren.8 9 However, their diagnostic performances, in terms of specificity, sensitivity and areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve, have been shown to vary considerably across different paediatric populations and age groups, particularly in young children aged less than 36 months old.10 11 Variability between studies can be attributed in part to differences in age group, definitions of SBIs adopted by different authors and the timings of presentation of these children to the emergency depart- ments.12 13 These biomarkers have been used for different diag- nostic purposes in SBI research. In using these biomarkers in clinical settings, clinicians apply different cut-­off values depending on whether we are trying to rule in or rule out SBIs. Most authors choose thresholds with high sensitivity and negative predictive values in view that SBIs should not be missed.14 15 In a systematic review by Van den Bruel et al, the authors recommended PCT level of 2 ng/mL and CRP of 80 mg/L to rule in serious infection, while lower thresholds of 0.5 ng/mL for PCT and 20 mg/L for CRP were recommended to rule out SBIs.14 Importantly, the diagnostic thresholds of these biomarkers reported in various studies vary widely, limiting direct application in other populations.16–18 In addition, different biomarkers have different kinetic profiles in that the levels of certain biomarkers such as IL-­6 rise faster than PCT and CRP, but have shorter half-­lives and can become undetectable within 24 hours.19 The diagnostic performances of these biomarkers therefore may vary significantly depending on the timing of presentation of these febrile children, which may in turn be affected by availability and accessi- bility of health services in different countries. In view of the evolving epidemiology of SBIs with high vaccination rates in many countries, it is also crucial to understand the performance of these biomarkers early (within 48 hours of presentation) in the course of infec- tion.20 21 To date, there have been no systematic reviews or meta-­analyses performed to assess the thresholds at which these biomarkers can accurately predict SBIs, nor their role in early detection of SBIs in febrile children aged ≤36 months old. Objectives The primary objective of this systematic review and meta-­ analysis is to determine the thresholds at which CRP, PCT and IL-­6 can perform optimally in distinguishing the presence of SBIs in children ≤36 months old presenting with fever without source. The secondary objective of the study is to determine their performances in early detection of SBIs within 48 hours of fever onset among children ≤36 months old presenting with fever without source. METHODS AND ANALYSIS We will report the systematic review and meta-­analysis in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-­Analyses (PRISMA) Diag- nostic Test Accuracy checklist.22 This review is registered with the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews with registration number CRD42023439093. Eligibility criteria We will identify, collate and review all available evidence from November 2013 to November 2023 reporting on the diagnostic accuracy of CRP, PCT and IL-­6 in detecting SBIs in children aged ≤36 months presenting with fever without apparent source that answer our clinical question, with the following population, intervention, comparator and outcome measures. Population: children aged ≤36 months presenting with fever without source; Intervention: CRP, PCT and/or IL-­6 performed as diag- nostic tools; Comparator: different biomarker thresholds; Outcomes: detection of SBIs. Randomised controlled trials (RCTs) and non-­ randomised studies including non-­RCTs, controlled before-­and-­after studies and cohort studies will be included. Case series, case–control studies, systematic reviews, conference abstracts, studies that include both paediatric and adult patients that do not report on the paediatric population separately as well as studies not reported in English will be excluded. We will also exclude studies with small population size (N<50) to prevent small-­study effects that may result from reporting biases and non-­generalisability,23 as well as those in specific high-­risk populations including studies that include patients with history of prematurity, immunodeficiencies and malignancies. Information sources We will systematically search electronic databases including MEDLINE, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, Cochrane CENTRAL, CINAHL (Cumulative Index to Nursing and Allied Health Liter- ature) and Science Citation Index. The bibliographies of all selected studies will be reviewed and screened for eligibility to ensure that our literature search is adequate. A manual Google search will be done too. Search strategy In collaboration with a librarian at our institution, we have developed an electronic search strategy involving the use of controlled vocabulary and keywords related to BMJ Paediatrics Open: first published as 10.1136/bmjpo-2023-002237 on 18 March 2024. First, the titles and abstracts of articles will be screened and reviewed to assess their relevance. Full-­text articles of all relevant articles will then be retrieved and assessed for eligibility based on inclu- sion and exclusion criteria. Two independent reviewers will independently screen and review the articles at both stages. Any disagreements will be resolved by a third inde- pendent reviewer or by consensus. Reasons for excluding studies will be recorded and tabulated in the appendix of the final report. Data extraction and synthesis Standardised data collection forms on Microsoft Excel will be used to extract relevant data from each included study independently by two researchers and then reconciled. The following data will be extracted from each article: study title, authors, publication date and year, type of publication, country, study design, sample size, inclusion and exclusion criteria, clinical setting, characteristics of study population (including age, gender, comorbidi- ties), duration of fever at the time of diagnostic workup and method of sampling CRP, PCT and IL-­6, values and units of measurement for CRP, PCT and IL-­6, diagnostic performance indicators from which a 2×2 table will be tabulated (true positives (TPs), true negatives (TNs), false positives (FPs) and false negatives (FNs)), presence of documented infections, definitions of SBIs, admis- sions and duration of hospitalisation, as well as antibiotic use. If clarifications are needed or additional data are required, we will email the original authors. If we receive no response within 3 weeks, a reminder email will be sent. The study will be excluded if we do not hear from the authors within 1 month. Definitions 1. Fever without source: temperature >38°C for less than 7 days without any signs or symptoms identifying source of infection. 2. Early presentation: presentation of febrile children to the emergency department within 48 hours of fever onset.25 3. SBI: presence of bacteraemia, urinary tract infection (UTI), pneumonia, bacterial meningitis, osteomyelitis or septic arthritis.26 27 4. Bacteraemia: growth of a single bacterial pathogen in blood, excluding growth of bacteria considered a pri- ori as contaminants, for example, coagulase-­negative Staphylococcus).28 5. UTI: growth of single urine pathogen with at least 50 000 colony-­forming units (CFUs)/mL from cath- eterised urine specimen; or 10 000–50 000 CFUs/mL from a catheterised specimen with positive urinalysis (positive for leucocyte esterase, nitrite or pyuria at >5 white blood cells; or at least 100 000 CFUs/mL from urine collected via voided specimens).29 6. Pneumonia: lobar consolidation diagnosed on chest radiography confirmed by a paediatric radiologist. 7. DISCUSSION While untreated bacterial infections may lead to signif- icant morbidity and mortality, overtreatment of self-­ limiting viral illnesses increases the risk of antibiotic resistance and contributes to higher healthcare costs.1 31 Differentiating children with SBIs from those with viral illnesses is therefore essential. Indeed, multiple studies have assessed the role of biomarkers in predicting SBIs in these children.9 32 CRP is an acute-­phase reactant produced in the hepato- cytes in response to tissue damage, infection or non-­specific immune system activation which can become elevated within 24 hours of a trigger, reach its maximum within 48 hours and has a half-­life of 24 hours.33–36 In contrast, PCT is a peptide precursor of the hormone calcitonin. Under normal physiology, only very small amount of PCT is released into circulation and its production increases rapidly within 6–12 hours and reaches its peak within 12 hours in response to bacterial endotoxins and inflamma- tory cytokines in extrathyroidal tissues, and has a half-­life of 24 hours.37 PCT has therefore been regarded as a more specific biomarker of systemic bacterial infection and sepsis, and has been reported to facilitate earlier diagnosis.37 38 On the other hand, IL-­6 is an inflammatory cytokine produced by monocytes and macrophages which rises early in the inflammatory cascade and functions as a hepatocyte-­ stimulating factor that enhances the production of acute-­ phase reactants including CRP.39 40 Although IL-­6 level rises sharply in response to infection, it falls rapidly with time and becomes undetectable within 24 hours.39 40 While the diagnostic performances of these biomarkers have been well reported and these biomarkers have been used to fortify existing clinical decision rules, their optimal thresholds remain inconclusive due to high vari- ability within and between studies. Additionally, their roles in early detection of SBIs for children presenting within 48 hours of fever onset are unclear. This system- atic review and meta-­analysis thus aims to determine the optimal thresholds at which biomarkers CRP, PCT and IL-­6 can predict SBIs in young children presenting with fever without source, as well as their early detection within 48 hours of fever onset. While multiple single-­ centre studies have been published on the diagnostic performances of these biomarkers, this systematic review and meta-­analysis will facilitate comprehensive analyses and reporting of biomarker thresholds. Our study has the potential to provide guidance on clinical decision-­ making in young children presenting with fever without source. Limitations Despite our best efforts in using a comprehensive search strategy, the keywords used may not yield all relevant articles. In addition, we will exclude all studies reported in languages other than English, which may reduce the generalisability of the findings. Given the nature of the study, we will not have access to individual patient-­level data which may render it impossible to study factors beyond those reported in published articles. In addi- tion, there may be heterogeneity in the thresholds of the biomarkers depending on the patient population and predominant pathogen within that population. ABSTRACT Introduction The management of fever without source in children ≤36 months old remains a diagnostic challenge as the underlying aetiologies can vary from self-­limiting viral infections to serious bacterial infections (SBIs). Biomarkers such as C reactive protein (CRP), procalcitonin (PCT) and interleukin-­6 (IL-­6) have varying thresholds in the prediction of SBIs due to differences in SBI definitions, SBI prevalence, patient characteristics and timing of presentation. This protocol describes a systematic review and meta-­analysis that aims to determine the thresholds at which CRP, PCT and IL-­6 can perform optimally in distinguishing the presence of SBIs in children ≤36 months old, as well as to determine their performances in early detection of bacterial infections within 48 hours of fever onset. Methods and analysis We will systematically search electronic databases including MEDLINE, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, Cochrane CENTRAL, EMBASE, CINAHL (Cumulative Index to Nursing and Allied Health Literature) and Science Citation Index from 1 July 2023 to 31 July 2023. We will include studies that report the diagnostic accuracy of CRP, PCT and IL-­6 in detecting SBIs in children aged ≤36 months presenting with fever without apparent source. Randomised controlled trials (RCTs) and non-­randomised studies including non-­RCTs and controlled before-­and-­after studies will be included. A meta-­analysis will be performed and diagnostic performances of these biomarkers will be reported. Ethics and dissemination The results of this study will provide guidance on clinical decision-­making in young children presenting with fever without source. Ethics approval will not be required for this study. The authors aim to publish the findings in a peer-­reviewed journal as well as present at international conferences. PROSPERO registration number CRD42023439093. The risk of missed diagnosis often leads to inappropriate prescribing of antibiotics, hospital admissions and unnecessary invasive testing.5 This clinical conundrum has led to an increasing volume of research into the role of biomarkers that aid clinicians in accurate and early diagnosis of SBIs. Among the biomarkers that have been evaluated, C reactive protein (CRP) and procalcitonin (PCT) have consistently been reported to be reliable predictors of SBIs in paediatric patients.6 7 Newer studies have also proposed the emerging role of cytokines, such as interleukin-­6 (IL-­6), in predicting sepsis in young chil- dren.8 9 However, their diagnostic performances, in terms of specificity, sensitivity and areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve, have been shown to vary considerably across different paediatric populations and age groups, particularly in young children aged less than 36 months old.10 11 Variability between studies can be attributed in part to differences in age group, definitions of SBIs adopted by different authors and the timings of presentation of these children to the emergency depart- ments.12 13 These biomarkers have been used for different diag- nostic purposes in SBI research. In using these biomarkers in clinical settings, clinicians apply different cut-­off values depending on whether we are trying to rule in or rule out SBIs. Most authors choose thresholds with high sensitivity and negative predictive values in view that SBIs should not be missed.14 15 In a systematic review by Van den Bruel et al, the authors recommended PCT level of 2 ng/mL and CRP of 80 mg/L to rule in serious infection, while lower thresholds of 0.5 ng/mL for PCT and 20 mg/L for CRP were recommended to rule out SBIs.14 Importantly, the diagnostic thresholds of these biomarkers reported in various studies vary widely, limiting direct application in other populations.16–18 In addition, different biomarkers have different kinetic profiles in that the levels of certain biomarkers such as IL-­6 rise faster than PCT and CRP, but have shorter half-­lives and can become undetectable within 24 hours.19 The diagnostic performances of these biomarkers therefore may vary significantly depending on the timing of presentation of these febrile children, which may in turn be affected by availability and accessi- bility of health services in different countries. In view of the evolving epidemiology of SBIs with high vaccination rates in many countries, it is also crucial to understand the performance of these biomarkers early (within 48 hours of presentation) in the course of infec- tion.20 21 To date, there have been no systematic reviews or meta-­analyses performed to assess the thresholds at which these biomarkers can accurately predict SBIs, nor their role in early detection of SBIs in febrile children aged ≤36 months old. Objectives The primary objective of this systematic review and meta-­ analysis is to determine the thresholds at which CRP, PCT and IL-­6 can perform optimally in distinguishing the presence of SBIs in children ≤36 months old presenting with fever without source. The secondary objective of the study is to determine their performances in early detection of SBIs within 48 hours of fever onset among children ≤36 months old presenting with fever without source. METHODS AND ANALYSIS We will report the systematic review and meta-­analysis in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-­Analyses (PRISMA) Diag- nostic Test Accuracy checklist.22 This review is registered with the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews with registration number CRD42023439093. Eligibility criteria We will identify, collate and review all available evidence from November 2013 to November 2023 reporting on the diagnostic accuracy of CRP, PCT and IL-­6 in detecting SBIs in children aged ≤36 months presenting with fever without apparent source that answer our clinical question, with the following population, intervention, comparator and outcome measures. Population: children aged ≤36 months presenting with fever without source; Intervention: CRP, PCT and/or IL-­6 performed as diag- nostic tools; Comparator: different biomarker thresholds; Outcomes: detection of SBIs. Randomised controlled trials (RCTs) and non-­ randomised studies including non-­RCTs, controlled before-­and-­after studies and cohort studies will be included. Case series, case–control studies, systematic reviews, conference abstracts, studies that include both paediatric and adult patients that do not report on the paediatric population separately as well as studies not reported in English will be excluded. We will also exclude studies with small population size (N<50) to prevent small-­study effects that may result from reporting biases and non-­generalisability,23 as well as those in specific high-­risk populations including studies that include patients with history of prematurity, immunodeficiencies and malignancies. Information sources We will systematically search electronic databases including MEDLINE, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, Cochrane CENTRAL, CINAHL (Cumulative Index to Nursing and Allied Health Liter- ature) and Science Citation Index. The bibliographies of all selected studies will be reviewed and screened for eligibility to ensure that our literature search is adequate. A manual Google search will be done too. Search strategy In collaboration with a librarian at our institution, we have developed an electronic search strategy involving the use of controlled vocabulary and keywords related to BMJ Paediatrics Open: first published as 10.1136/bmjpo-2023-002237 on 18 March 2024. All analyses will be carried out using SAS V.9.4, Meta-­DiSc V.1.4 and R V.4.2.2 (2022-­10-­31 ucrt). All tests will be two sided and p<0.05 will be considered as statistically significant. DISCUSSION While untreated bacterial infections may lead to signif- icant morbidity and mortality, overtreatment of self-­ limiting viral illnesses increases the risk of antibiotic resistance and contributes to higher healthcare costs.1 31 Differentiating children with SBIs from those with viral illnesses is therefore essential. Indeed, multiple studies have assessed the role of biomarkers in predicting SBIs in these children.9 32 CRP is an acute-­phase reactant produced in the hepato- cytes in response to tissue damage, infection or non-­specific immune system activation which can become elevated within 24 hours of a trigger, reach its maximum within 48 hours and has a half-­life of 24 hours.33–36 In contrast, PCT is a peptide precursor of the hormone calcitonin. Under normal physiology, only very small amount of PCT is released into circulation and its production increases rapidly within 6–12 hours and reaches its peak within 12 hours in response to bacterial endotoxins and inflamma- tory cytokines in extrathyroidal tissues, and has a half-­life of 24 hours.37 PCT has therefore been regarded as a more specific biomarker of systemic bacterial infection and sepsis, and has been reported to facilitate earlier diagnosis.37 38 On the other hand, IL-­6 is an inflammatory cytokine produced by monocytes and macrophages which rises early in the inflammatory cascade and functions as a hepatocyte-­ stimulating factor that enhances the production of acute-­ phase reactants including CRP.39 40 Although IL-­6 level rises sharply in response to infection, it falls rapidly with time and becomes undetectable within 24 hours.39 40 While the diagnostic performances of these biomarkers have been well reported and these biomarkers have been used to fortify existing clinical decision rules, their optimal thresholds remain inconclusive due to high vari- ability within and between studies. Additionally, their roles in early detection of SBIs for children presenting within 48 hours of fever onset are unclear. This system- atic review and meta-­analysis thus aims to determine the optimal thresholds at which biomarkers CRP, PCT and IL-­6 can predict SBIs in young children presenting with fever without source, as well as their early detection within 48 hours of fever onset. While multiple single-­ centre studies have been published on the diagnostic performances of these biomarkers, this systematic review and meta-­analysis will facilitate comprehensive analyses and reporting of biomarker thresholds. Our study has the potential to provide guidance on clinical decision-­ making in young children presenting with fever without source. Limitations Despite our best efforts in using a comprehensive search strategy, the keywords used may not yield all relevant articles. In addition, we will exclude all studies reported in languages other than English, which may reduce the generalisability of the findings. Given the nature of the study, we will not have access to individual patient-­level data which may render it impossible to study factors beyond those reported in published articles. In addi- tion, there may be heterogeneity in the thresholds of the biomarkers depending on the patient population and predominant pathogen within that population.
